let μ := Measure.infinitePi (fun _ : ℕ => ProbabilityTheory.cond (Measure.count : Measure (ℤ × ℤ)) steps)
  let inc (i : ℕ) (w : ℕ → ℤ × ℤ) := w i
  let peak (n : ℕ) (w : ℕ → ℤ × ℤ) := (Finset.range (n+1)).sup fun i =>
    localTime inc n w (position inc i w)
  let hit (m k : ℕ) : Set (ℕ → ℤ × ℤ) := {w | ∃ n, peak n w = m ∧
    (k : ℕ∞) ≤ (favouriteSites inc n w).encard}
  ∃ b : ℕ → ℕ, (∑' j : ℕ, μ {w | ¬ ∃ m ∈ Finset.Icc j (b j), w ∈ hit m 3}) ≠ ∞

lead.title: Erdős Problem 1165 · step 1

review.statement: For the IID uniform nearest-neighbor walk on ℤ² started at the origin, count visits at times 0 through n inclusive. Write peak(n,w) for the largest local time and F(n,w) for the set of sites attaining it. The supplied target asks for one deterministic function b : ℕ → ℕ such that the sum over j ∈ ℕ of the probabilities of the following failure is finite: there are no m,n ∈ ℕ with j ≤ m ≤ b(j), peak(n,w) = m, and |F(n,w)| ≥ 3. The parent problem asks, for every integer r ≥ 3, for the probability that for every N there exists n ≥ N with |F(n,w)| = r.
review.significance: The window bound lets the first Borel–Cantelli lemma give a three-or-more-way tie at a peak level in [j,b(j)] for every sufficiently large j, almost surely. The supplied formula leaves the growth of b unrestricted.
review.settlement_test: For the supplied formula, it suffices to prove that almost surely, for every j there is a time n with peak(n,w) ≥ j and |F(n,w)| ≥ 3. Measurable continuity then gives deterministic endpoints with a geometric bound on the failure probabilities. For formal settlement, independently replay a proof of the exact queue declaration with its imports and hypotheses and audit the resulting axioms.
review.aliases: Erdős–Révész favourite values problem, planar favorite sites problem, simultaneous maximizers of local time, Erdős Problem 1165, and item 6.77 in Some of Paul's favorite problems. [Original booklet](https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~vjekovac/EP/Some_of_Pauls_favorite_problems.pdf)

review.proof_or_witness:
Candidate mathematical proof. For any j ≥ 1, divide the IID increments into disjoint blocks of length 2j. The block consisting of j repetitions of ((1,0),(-1,0)) has probability 4^(-2j). The probability of missing it in N blocks is (1−4^(-2j))^N, which tends to zero. A matching block gives j+1 visits to its starting site, including both endpoints. Intersecting over j gives an almost surely unbounded peak. The peak is nondecreasing because every site's local time is nondecreasing. Theorem 1.1 supplies arbitrarily late times with exactly three favourites almost surely. Together these statements give, for every j, a time with peak at least j and at least three favourites.

Fix j and set A(j,B) = ⋃_{j≤m≤B} hit(m,3). The time-n event is determined by the first n increments, so it is a countable union of measurable cylinders. Taking the countable union over n gives measurability of hit(m,3). As B increases, A(j,B) increases to an event of measure one. Therefore μ(A(j,B)ᶜ) tends to zero. Take b(j) to be the least B ≥ j with μ(A(j,B)ᶜ) ≤ 2^(-(j+1)). The required sum is at most 1. The argument is preserved in the isolated notebook. [Theorem 1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.00995v2), [research-notebook.md](/private/var/folders/kp/0gn1clkj59g9nzk16977plmh0000gn/T/tmp79ezfjsw/work/research-notebook.md)
review.remaining_obligation: The exact intermediate Lean lemma is `∀ᵐ w ∂μ, ∀ j : ℕ, ∃ n : ℕ, j ≤ peak n w ∧ (3 : ℕ∞) ≤ (favouriteSites inc n w).encard`. To establish it using the existing formal proof, show that mapping the IID `Fin 4` direction sequence coordinatewise to its lattice displacements gives the conditioned-counting product law μ. Identify the trajectories, time-zero-inclusive local times, and favourite cardinalities, then formalize peak unboundedness and the measurable window argument. I did not produce a full Lean file or run an independent kernel replay.
